title: Order-ready text messages for pickup customers
description: Write an order-ready text message that tells pickup customers when to come in and what to expect. Keep the process quick for staff and guests.
question: What should I send in an order ready text for pickup customers?
answer: Send a short text that says the order is ready, where to pick it up, and any simple pickup instruction like the name to give at the counter. Keep it clear and practical, and do not include payment requests if you already take payment at pickup. If you use ROAL, it can quote pickup times on the call, and your team can still handle the handoff at the counter.
summary: You’ll know how to write and time pickup-ready texts that reduce confusion at the counter.
intro:
An order ready text for pickup customers should be short, clear, and easy to act on. It should tell the guest their order is ready, where to come in, and what name to give at pickup.

For a busy restaurant, the goal is simple: less waiting, fewer “is my food done?” calls, and a cleaner handoff at the counter. That matters whether you take pickup orders by phone, online, or through an AI phone host like ROAL.

sections.h2: What should an order ready text pickup message say?
sections.body:
A good ready text does three jobs: it confirms the order is done, tells the guest exactly where to go, and gives one simple action. Do not make the customer read a long paragraph while standing in the parking lot.

Use this basic structure:

1. Say the order is ready.
2. Give the pickup spot.
3. Tell them the name to use.
4. Add one detail only if it helps, like “come to the side door” or “ring the bell.”

Example text:
> “Hi Maria, your pickup order is ready at Bella Pizza. Please come to the front counter and give the name Maria.”

If your setup is different, swap in your own details:
- “Please use the side entrance.”
- “Pickup is at the takeout window.”
- “Ask for the order under James.”

Keep it consistent. If your team sends five different versions, customers get confused. A simple standard line works better than a clever one.

sections.h2: When should you send the text so the customer arrives at the right time?
sections.body:
Send the text when the order is actually ready, not when the kitchen starts cooking it. If you text too early, the guest shows up too soon and stands around. If you text too late, the food sits and gets cold.

A workable routine for a small shop is:

1. Kitchen marks the order ready.
2. Front counter or host sends the text right away.
3. Staff keeps the pickup area clear for the next few minutes.
4. If the customer does not come in, you wait a short window before follow-up.

A practical example: say you quote a 20-minute ready time for a $28 pickup order. If the kitchen is running on time, the ready text goes out at minute 20. If it runs 5 minutes late, send it when the order is actually packed and labeled.

That timing matters even more on busy nights. If your phone team is tied up, [pickup order taking](/use-cases/pickup-orders) can still stay organized when the caller gets a quoted ready time and the kitchen has a clear ticket.

sections.h2: How do you keep pickup texts short without sounding cold?
sections.body:
You do not need a warm paragraph to sound polite. A clean, direct text feels professional and saves time.

Try this tone:
- Friendly greeting
- One sentence about readiness
- One sentence about pickup instructions
- No extra chatter

Examples you can copy and adjust:
- “Hi Tony, your order is ready now. Please pick it up at the front counter and give the name Tony.”
- “Hi, your takeout order is ready. Use the side entrance for pickup.”
- “Your order is ready for pickup. Please ask for the order under Priya at the register.”

Avoid messages like:
- “We are pleased to inform you…”
- “Your culinary experience awaits…”
- “Kindly proceed to the establishment…”

Those lines waste time and feel stiff. Your customers want clear instructions, not a speech. If you already use ROAL, it can collect the caller’s name and phone number and confirm the order back on the call, which helps the ready text feel like the final step instead of the first time the guest hears the details.

sections.h2: What details should your pickup text include, and what should you leave out?
sections.body:
The best pickup text includes only the details the customer needs at the counter. Too much information creates confusion, especially when people are in a hurry or juggling kids, parking, and traffic.

Use this checklist for every order-ready text pickup message:

- Customer name
- Order is ready now
- Pickup location or entrance
- Any simple counter instruction
- Optional note if the guest requested curbside or a specific door

Leave out these items unless they are truly needed:
- Menu details
- Long apologies
- Payment requests if payment happens at pickup
- Kitchen explanations
- Staff names that do not help the customer

If you want a more complete handoff, keep that on the ticket and in your kitchen screen, not in the text. ROAL sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen, while the ready text can stay short and customer-facing.

| Include | Leave out |
|---|---|
| “Ready now” | “We experienced a slight delay in the sauté station” |
| “Front counter” | Long kitchen notes |
| “Ask for Sam” | Menu reminders |
| “Side door” | Payment instructions, if you already collect at pickup |

Short wins. A pickup guest usually just wants to move fast, grab the food, and get back on the road.

sections.h2: How can you reduce repeat calls asking, ‘Is my order ready?’
sections.body:
The easiest way to cut those calls is to pair a clear quoted ready time with a clean ready text. When the customer knows what to expect, they are less likely to call back early.

A simple phone script helps:
> “Your pickup order should be ready in about 20 minutes. We’ll text you when it’s ready.”

That line works because it sets a clear expectation. Then the ready text closes the loop. If a guest still calls, your staff can answer quickly because the order details are already in one place.

Here is a simple workflow for a takeout-heavy night:

1. Take the order.
2. Confirm the name and phone number.
3. Quote the ready time.
4. Send the ready text when the order is packed.
5. Mark the ticket as ready so the counter team sees it.

If you want to compare this with human coverage or monthly phone plans, [pay per order vs monthly AI phone plans](/compare/monthly-ai-phone-plans) is useful reading. For some restaurants, the big win is not just answering calls. It is keeping the whole pickup flow cleaner from the first ring to the final handoff.

sections.h2: What should restaurants do if the pickup order is late or not claimed?
sections.body:
Sometimes the order is ready and the guest is not there yet. Sometimes the guest says they are five minutes away and that turns into fifteen. Your text should still stay simple, but your team needs a basic backup plan.

Use a short internal rule like this:

1. Text when ready.
2. Hold the order in the usual pickup spot.
3. If the guest does not arrive after a reasonable wait, make one follow-up call or text.
4. Keep notes on the ticket if the order was delayed, remade, or picked up late.

Example follow-up text:
> “Hi Maria, your order has been ready for pickup. Please come to the front counter when you arrive.”

Do not overdo the follow-up. One reminder is enough in most cases. If the order has special handling, like a allergy-sensitive request, keep the details with staff and not in the text.

ROAL can help by handing tricky calls to staff with a summary, while the regular pickup order still gets into the kitchen cleanly. For owners dealing with high call volume, that separation matters more than fancy wording.

sections.h2: How do you set this up without adding another task to your staff?
sections.body:
Your team does not need another complicated system. You need one repeatable process that the host, counter staff, and kitchen all understand.

A simple setup looks like this:

1. The caller places the order by phone.
2. The phone host takes the items, sizes, modifiers, notes, name, and phone.
3. The kitchen screen shows the ticket.
4. Staff packs the order and marks it ready.
5. The ready text goes out using your standard wording.

If you use ROAL, the owner can paste the restaurant website, Google Maps link, or “Name, City” at /try, and ROAL reads the menu, prices, hours, and address from public pages. The owner can test-call it in the browser first, then go live by forwarding the restaurant’s number to the host. That makes the pickup flow easier to manage without changing your public number.

A practical checklist before you launch:
- Decide the exact ready text line.
- Decide where pickup happens.
- Decide who marks orders ready.
- Decide what happens when someone is late.
- Test the wording with one real order.

If you want to start from a simple phone setup, [build a free test host](/try) and try your own pickup wording before you use it on a busy shift.

takeaways: A pickup-ready text should be short, clear, and tied to the actual ready time.
Include only the name, pickup spot, and one simple instruction.
Use one standard message so every staff member sends the same wording.
Keep payment out of the text if you already take payment at pickup.
A clean ready text works best when the kitchen ticket and pickup process are organized too.

faq.q: What is the best text for pickup orders being ready?
faq.a: The best text is short and direct: say the order is ready, name the pickup spot, and tell the guest what name to give. For example: “Hi Lena, your pickup order is ready at the front counter. Please give the name Lena.” Keep it simple so the customer can act on it quickly.

faq.q: Should I text pickup customers before or after the food is ready?
faq.a: Text them after the food is actually ready. If you send the message too early, the guest may arrive before the kitchen has finished packing the order. A clean ready text sent at the right moment reduces confusion and extra calls.

faq.q: Can I include payment instructions in the pickup ready text?
faq.a: Only if your restaurant already uses that process and it helps the pickup handoff. ROAL does not take card numbers over the phone, and payment happens at pickup or however your restaurant already takes it. In most cases, the ready text should focus on pickup instructions, not payment.

faq.q: How can ROAL help with pickup order texts?
faq.a: ROAL answers the phone, takes pickup orders from your live menu, confirms the order, and sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. That makes the pickup workflow easier because the name, phone number, items, and ready time are already captured on the call before the order-ready text goes out.
